newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CROWN UNDER PRESSURE AS GOVT PONDERS RESHUFFLE.
newsitem.headline: CROWN UNDER PRESSURE AS GOVT PONDERS RESHUFFLE.

text.p: Speculators kept the Czech crown under severe pressure on Wednesday, while political leaders pondered a reshuffle to restore credibility to the beleaguered government.

The crown, which has been under selling pressure for more than a week on investor alarm at political uncertainty and a severe economic downturn, plunged to a new low in early trade, prompting fresh central bank action to defend the currency.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said the crown's fall was a result of the "nervous situation" on the political scene and to opposition demands for a change in economic course.

"I expect to take a number of clear actions. I have also talked about it with Mr President (Vaclav Havel). I'm persuaded that the coalition leaders who will show readiness to continue further in an unaltered economic course will be a stabilising factor," he said.

The central bank, which had in recent days directly intervened and sharply raised interest rates to support the crown, decided to limit non-residents' access to the Czech money market and shut off access to the last-resort Lombard credit facility and raised short-term rates even further.
"This is not a reaction to events only this morning but to the situation that non-residents are taking big positions on the money market," bank board member Ludek Niedermeyer said.

The crown, which had earlier weakened to a new low of 6.4 percent below the mid-point of the dollar/mark basket against which it is fixed, immediately strengthened on the move but remained volatile. The currency stood at around -4.0 percent percent below parity at 1330 GMT.
Klaus told Czech Radio he would contact central bank governor Josef Tosvsky to discuss what "symbolic" action to take to help the crown.
Both the government and central bank have ruled out the devaluation which some analysts now say is inevitable.
But asked in a meeting with foreign journalists whether the cabinet had recently discussed the possiblity of a devaluation, Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy said: "Not at all."

Leaders of the coalition parties were to meet during the day to discuss a government reshuffle agreed in principle on Wednesday. That decision followed a wave of criticism and internal coalition tension over the economic situation.
Dlouhy, whose Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA) party supports a reconstruction of the cabinet, said the reshuffle could take a few hours or until the end of next month.
Some analysts have said the centre-right government, and Klaus in particular, have run out of ideas.
"He has his responsibility, as we all have, including responsibility for the fact that the government does not look as if it is acting," Dlouhy said.
However, he said the government had acted last month when it unveiled a package of measures to kick-start growth and curb burgeoning trade and current account deficits.
Dlouhy, who declined detailed comment on the battle over the crown, said the pressure on the currency was due to the time lag in the government measures taking effect.

"It seems that for the moment the crown will stabilise but it may stabilise at a lower level which as a trade minister for the moment I would not mind," Dlouhy said, speaking before the latest round of attacks by speculators on the currency.
He denied the economy was in crisis and said preliminary April trade data, showing a narrowing of the trade gap to 11 billion crowns from 13-14 billion in the first quarter, was a positive sign.
